lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Welding is a skill that can put food on your table every day if you treat it like a business, not just a job. In many African cities and towns, there is a constant demand for welding services: gates, window frames, burglar bars, wheelbarrows, ox-carts, and repairs for cars, trucks, and farm equipment. But most welders stay poor because they only sell their time by the hour and never build a business. This module will show you how to turn your welding skills into a profitable enterprise that can grow and employ others.

Why does running a welding business matter? Because Africa is building fast. New houses, schools, shops, and roads are going up everywhere. Every building needs metalwork. Every truck and taxi needs repairs. If you can organise yourself, buy the right tools, price your work correctly, and keep customers happy, you can earn far more than a daily wage. You can also create jobs for other young people in your community.

Running a welding business is not just about striking an arc. You need to find customers, quote jobs, buy materials at good prices, manage cash flow, and keep records. You need to understand your costs: electrodes, gas, steel, grinding discs, electricity or diesel, transport, and your own time. Many welders fail because they charge too little, don't separate business money from personal money, or take on jobs without a deposit.

This module covers the practical steps: the tools and materials you need to start, a step-by-step method to set up and run your business, common mistakes and how to fix them, safety and best practices, and a practical exercise to get you started. By the end, you will have a clear plan to turn your welding skills into a steady income. Remember: a welder who understands business will always have work, while a welder who only knows welding may struggle. Let's get started.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To run a welding business, you need more than just a welding machine. You need a full set of tools and a reliable supply of materials. Start with the basics: a welding machine. For most small workshops in Africa, a 200-amp inverter welder that runs on 220V single-phase is ideal. It can weld up to 4mm electrodes and is portable. If you don't have electricity, consider a diesel generator of at least 5kVA, but remember fuel costs. You also need an angle grinder (115mm or 230mm) with cutting and grinding discs, a chipping hammer, a wire brush, a set of files, a measuring tape, a square, a spirit level, a centre punch, and a good workbench. For safety, you need a welding helmet (auto-darkening is best), leather gloves, apron, safety boots, and goggles for grinding.

Materials are your biggest ongoing cost. You will need mild steel rods (electrodes) in sizes 2.5mm and 3.2mm, and possibly 4mm for heavy work. Buy in bulk from a steel merchant to get a discount. Common steel sections include square tubing (20x20mm, 25x25mm, 40x40mm), rectangular tubing, round tubing, angle iron, flat bar, and sheet metal. Keep a stock of common sizes so you can start jobs immediately. Also stock grinding discs, cutting discs, paint (red oxide primer and enamel), and anti-rust treatment.

You will need a way to transport materials and finished products. A small pickup truck or a three-wheeled cargo bike is useful. If you can't afford one, build a simple handcart. For mobile jobs, you need a portable welding machine and a long extension cable. A basic tool kit for on-site repairs should include a generator, grinder, and hand tools.

Finally, set up a small workshop. It can be a rented space, a corner of your compound, or a roadside stall. Ensure it has a strong table, a vice, a place to store steel, and good ventilation. You don't need everything at once. Start with the essentials and reinvest profits to buy more tools. Many successful welders started with just a machine, a grinder, and a hammer. The key is to keep your tools in good condition and always have materials ready so you never turn away a customer.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Register your business. Even a small welding business should be registered. In most African countries, you can register a business name at the local government office or online. This allows you to open a bank account, get a tax number, and bid for bigger contracts. It also makes you look professional. Keep the registration certificate and receipts safe.

Step 2: Find a good location. You need a place that is visible and accessible. Near a main road, a market, or a growing residential area is ideal. If you can't afford rent, start at home but put up a signboard. Make sure you have enough space for a workbench, steel storage, and parking for customers.

Step 3: Set your prices. Calculate your costs: materials, labour, electricity, transport, and a profit margin. For example, if a gate uses 50kg of steel at 20 birr/kg (or equivalent), that's 1000 birr. Add electrodes, grinding discs, paint, and 2 days of your labour at 500 birr/day = 1000 birr. Total cost = 2200 birr. Add 30% profit = 2860 birr. Quote 2900 birr. Always give a written quote and take a 50% deposit before buying materials.

Step 4: Market your business. Tell everyone you know. Put up a signboard with your phone number. Use social media like WhatsApp, Facebook, and TikTok to post photos of your work. Offer a small discount for referrals. Visit hardware stores, car repair garages, and construction sites to introduce yourself. Word of mouth is powerful: do good work and ask happy customers to recommend you.

Step 5: Manage your money. Open a separate bank account or mobile money account for the business. Pay yourself a fixed salary each week. Keep receipts for all purchases. Track every job: what you charged, what you spent, and your profit. Use a simple notebook or a free app like Wave or Keeper. Never mix business money with personal money.

Step 6: Deliver quality and on time. Always finish jobs when you promised. If you can't, communicate early. Check your welds: they should be strong, clean, and free of slag. Grind smooth and paint to prevent rust. A satisfied customer will return and tell others. A bad job will ruin your reputation.

Step 7: Grow slowly. Reinvest profits into better tools, more materials, and training. Hire an apprentice when you have more work than you can handle. Teach them properly and pay them fairly. Consider adding services like gate automation, aluminium welding, or mobile repairs. Keep learning new techniques. With discipline, your one-man workshop can become a thriving business.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Charging too little. Many welders quote low prices to win jobs, then struggle to buy materials or pay themselves. Fix: Calculate your costs properly and add a fair profit. Never work for free. If a customer says your price is too high, explain the quality and warranty you offer. It's better to lose a job than to lose money.

Mistake 2: No deposit. If you buy materials with your own money and the customer refuses to pay, you lose. Fix: Always ask for at least 50% deposit before starting. For large jobs, ask for 50% upfront and 50% on delivery. Put the agreement in writing, even if it's just a handwritten note signed by both parties.

Mistake 3: Mixing business and personal money. You buy steel with the money meant for school fees, then you can't pay fees. Fix: Open a separate business account. Pay yourself a fixed weekly or monthly salary. Keep all business transactions separate.

Mistake 4: Poor record keeping. You don't know if you made a profit or loss. Fix: Write down every job: date, customer, description, amount charged, materials used, and expenses. Use a simple notebook or a free app. At the end of each month, add up your income and expenses to see your profit.

Mistake 5: Ignoring safety. You weld without a helmet and get eye damage, or you don't wear gloves and get burned. Fix: Always wear proper PPE: welding helmet, gloves, apron, safety boots, and goggles for grinding. Keep a fire extinguisher or bucket of sand nearby. Ventilate your workspace.

Mistake 6: Taking on jobs you can't do. You promise a complex aluminium weld but you only know mild steel. Fix: Be honest. If you can't do it, refer the customer to someone who can, or ask for time to learn. You can also partner with a more experienced welder.

Mistake 7: Not maintaining tools. A grinder with a worn cable shocks you, or a welding machine overheats. Fix: Inspect tools daily. Replace damaged cables, clean the machine, and service the generator regularly. A small maintenance cost prevents big repair bills.

Mistake 8: Poor customer service. You arrive late, don't answer calls, or deliver shoddy work. Fix: Answer your phone, be polite, and deliver on time. If you can't, communicate. A happy customer is your best advertisement.

Mistake 9: Giving up too soon. Business is slow at first. Fix: Persist. Keep marketing, improve your skills, and save. Most successful welders took at least a year to build a steady customer base. Don't quit.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety is not optional. As a welder, you face hazards every day: electric shock, burns, eye damage, fumes, and fire. In Africa, many welders work in informal settings without proper protection. This must change. Always wear personal protective equipment (PPE). A welding helmet with a proper shade lens (shade 10-13 for arc welding) protects your eyes from arc flash. Leather gloves, a leather apron, and safety boots protect your skin from sparks and hot metal. When grinding, wear goggles and a face shield. Never weld in shorts or open shoes.

Ventilation is critical. Welding fumes contain toxic metals and gases. Work in an open area or use a fan to blow fumes away. If you weld inside, install an exhaust hood or weld near an open door. Never weld in a closed room with no airflow. If you feel dizzy or nauseous, stop and get fresh air immediately.

Prevent fires. Welding sparks can travel up to 10 metres and ignite flammable materials. Clear your workspace of paper, cloth, petrol, and paint thinners. Keep a fire extinguisher (dry powder or CO2) or a bucket of sand and water nearby. Never weld near fuel tanks or gas cylinders. After welding, stay in the area for at least 30 minutes to watch for smoldering fires.

Electrical safety. Check your welding machine and cables for damage before use. Never touch the electrode or work clamp with bare hands when the machine is on. Ensure proper grounding. Use a circuit breaker. If you use a generator, place it outdoors and refuel only when it's off and cool.

Best practices for quality work: Prepare metal before welding. Clean off rust, paint, and oil with a grinder or wire brush. Fit parts properly with clamps and tack welds. Use the correct electrode and amperage for the metal thickness. For 3mm steel, use 2.5mm electrode at 70-90 amps; for 6mm steel, use 3.2mm at 100-130 amps. Weld in a steady, consistent motion. Remove slag after each pass. Inspect your welds: they should be smooth, with no undercut, porosity, or cracks. If you find a defect, grind it out and re-weld.

Keep your workspace organised. Store steel and tools safely. Put away cables to avoid tripping. Clean up at the end of each day. A clean workshop is a safe workshop. Finally, get first aid training. Know how to treat burns, cuts, and eye injuries. Keep a first aid kit with burn cream, bandages, and eye wash. Your safety and the safety of others depend on your habits.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it's time to put everything into practice. This exercise will guide you through setting up a simple welding business plan and completing a real job from start to finish. Follow these steps:

1. Write a one-page business plan. Include: business name, location, services offered (e.g., gates, window frames, repairs), target customers, and your prices for common items. For example, a standard 3m gate might be 8000 birr, a window frame 1500 birr, and a small repair 500 birr. Use the pricing method from Lesson 3.

2. Calculate your startup costs. List tools you already have and tools you need to buy. For example: inverter welder (15,000 birr), angle grinder (3,000 birr), helmet (1,500 birr), gloves (500 birr), measuring tape (200 birr), square (300 birr). Total needed: 20,500 birr. If you don't have all, start with the essentials and borrow or rent the rest.

3. Find your first customer. Talk to neighbours, friends, and local businesses. Offer a small job at a fair price. For example, repair a broken gate or make a simple burglar bar for a window. Agree on a price, take a 50% deposit, and buy materials.

4. Do the job safely and well. Wear your PPE. Measure twice, cut once. Weld strong joints. Grind smooth. Paint with red oxide primer and enamel. Clean up. Take before and after photos.

5. Get paid and record the job. Collect the remaining 50%. Write down in your notebook: date, customer, job description, amount charged, materials cost, and profit. For example: gate repair, charged 800 birr, materials 200 birr, profit 600 birr.

6. Ask for a testimonial. If the customer is happy, ask them to write a short recommendation or to tell friends. Take a photo of the finished work and post it on WhatsApp or Facebook with your phone number.

7. Review and improve. After the job, ask yourself: What went well? What could be better? Did I make a profit? Adjust your prices or methods for next time.

8. Repeat. Do at least three jobs this month. Each job will teach you something new. Keep records of all jobs. At the end of the month, calculate your total profit. Reinvest part of it into a new tool or more materials.

This exercise is your launchpad. Many successful welding businesses started with one small job and grew through word of mouth. Be reliable, do quality work, and manage your money. Within six months, you can have a steady stream of customers and a growing business. Good luck!

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Running a Welding Business in Africa

This practical reference consolidates the core operating knowledge you need to run a welding business profitably in an African context. It is business-first: every tool, table, and checklist below is framed around winning work, pricing it correctly, delivering on time, and protecting your margin. Use it as a bench-side manual you return to before quoting a job, buying equipment, or training a new hand.

Welding demand across Africa is driven by construction, mining, agriculture, transport, and informal manufacturing. In many markets, the barrier to entry is low â a machine, a mask, and a generator can start a business â but the barrier to staying in business is high. The welders who survive are those who treat the craft as a business: they know their cost per hour, they standardise their consumables, they quote from data rather than guesswork, and they never compromise on safety.

1. Setting Your Shop Rate: The Numbers That Decide Profit

Most welding businesses in Africa fail not because the welds are bad, but because the price is wrong. Before quoting any job, you must know your all-in cost per hour. The table below gives a realistic structure for a small urban workshop in a market such as Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, or Johannesburg. Adjust the figures to your own currency and location â the structure is what matters.

Table 1: Indicative monthly cost structure for a small welding workshop (1â2 welders)
Cost category Typical share of total cost Notes for African operators
Labour (wages, own draw)30â40%Include your own salary â many owners forget this and underprice.
Consumables (electrodes, wire, gas, tips)15â25%Buy in bulk where possible; import delays raise unit cost.
Power (grid or generator fuel)8â15%Load-shedding means generator fuel is a real line item, not a rounding error.
Equipment depreciation & maintenance5â10%Set aside a replacement fund monthly; machines do not last forever.
Premises / rent / storage5â12%Secure storage reduces theft of copper, gas, and tools.
Transport & site mobilisation3â8%Charge for it explicitly; do not absorb it into the weld price.
Overheads (airtime, data, licences, insurance)5â10%Compliance costs are rising; budget for them.
Profit margin15â25%Without this, you are buying yourself a job, not building a business.

Source: Cost structure adapted from ILO small enterprise development guidance and African Development Bank SME finance publications. Percentages are indicative and vary by country and market segment.

2. Consumables and Materials Reference

Consumable selection is where technical skill meets business discipline. The wrong electrode wastes time, causes rework, and destroys your reputation. The table below maps common African job types to recommended consumables and typical applications.

Table 2: Common welding processes, consumables, and African job applications
Process Consumable Typical use in African markets Key business consideration
SMAW (stick)E6013, E7018 electrodesGates, burglar bars, trailers, general repairCheapest entry point; works off generator power.
MIG/MAGER70S-6 wire + shielding gasFurniture frames, vehicle bodies, production runsHigher output but needs reliable power and gas supply.
TIGER5356 / ER4043 filler rodsAluminium windows, stainless steel kitchen equipment, dairyPremium pricing; requires clean, skilled work.
Oxy-acetyleneOxygen + acetyleneCutting, heating, brazing, rural repair workHigh gas cost; theft risk â secure cylinders.
FCAWFlux-cored wireHeavy structural steel, outdoor site workWind-tolerant; good for construction sites.

Source: Process and consumable classifications based on American Welding Society (AWS) standards and ISO 2553 / ISO 4063 welding process standards. Applications adapted to common African SME market segments.

3. Pricing a Job: The Step-by-Step Method

Use this sequence every time you quote. It prevents the two most common pricing errors: forgetting overheads, and underestimating consumable waste.

  1. Measure the work. Count joints, metres of weld, and thickness. Do not quote from memory.
  2. Estimate time. Use past jobs. A 1-metre butt weld on 6mm steel typically takes 15â25 minutes including setup and clean-up.
  3. Calculate consumables. Electrodes, gas, wire, grinding discs, and anti-spatter. Add 10â15% waste allowance.
  4. Add labour at your true hourly rate (from Table 1, not the casual daily rate).
  5. Add overheads as a percentage â typically 10â20% of direct cost.
  6. Add profit margin (15â25%). This is not optional.
  7. Add transport and mobilisation if the job is off-site.
  8. Present the quote in writing with scope, exclusions, payment terms, and validity period. Verbal quotes are how disputes start.
â  SAFETY WARNING â DO NOT WELD WITHOUT FULL PPE AND VENTILATION

Arc welding produces intense ultraviolet and infrared radiation that can permanently damage eyes and skin within seconds. Welding fumes â especially from galvanised, painted, or stainless steel â contain manganese, hexavalent chromium, and zinc oxide, which cause serious long-term lung and neurological harm. In many African workshops, welding is done in enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces without fume extraction. This is unacceptable. Minimum requirements: auto-darkening or fixed-shade helmet (shade 10â13), leather gloves, flame-resistant apron, safety boots, and eye protection for everyone in the area. Use local exhaust ventilation or weld outdoors. Never weld on sealed containers or near fuel. Keep a dry-powder fire extinguisher within reach. If you cannot provide PPE, you cannot legally or ethically run this business.

4. Common Business Mistakes and Fixes

Mistake 1: Pricing by the job instead of by the hour. Fix: build a simple spreadsheet or notebook that tracks hours and consumables per job for three months, then set rates from data.

Mistake 2: No written quotes or contracts. Fix: use a one-page quote template with scope, price, deposit, and completion date. Even a WhatsApp PDF counts.

Mistake 3: Mixing business and personal cash. Fix: open a separate business account or mobile-money wallet. Pay yourself a fixed monthly amount.

Mistake 4: Buying cheap consumables to save money. Fix: cheap electrodes cause porosity, rework, and lost clients. Buy from authorised distributors and keep batch records.

Mistake 5: Ignoring maintenance. Fix: schedule weekly machine checks, keep spare tips and liners, and budget 5â10% of revenue for repairs and replacement.

Mistake 6: No safety culture. Fix: make PPE a condition of employment, train every new hand, and display safety rules in the workshop. Insurance and client audits increasingly require this.

5. Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Know your hourly cost â labour, power, consumables, overheads, and depreciation combined.
  • â Quote in writing with scope, exclusions, price, deposit, and completion date.
  • â Add 10â15% consumable waste and 15â25% profit margin to every job.
  • â Charge transport separately â never absorb site mobilisation into the weld price.
  • â Keep a job log of hours, materials, and rework for every project.
  • â Maintain PPE and ventilation as non-negotiable operating conditions.
  • â Separate business and personal finances â pay yourself a fixed salary.
  • â Set aside 5â10% of revenue monthly for equipment replacement and insurance.

6. Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • TWI (The Welding Institute) â Job Knowledge technical library â free welding process and best-practice articles.
  • American Welding Society (AWS) â Standards and publications â process classifications and safety references.
  • OSHA â Welding, Cutting, and Brazing safety guidance â free, practical hazard controls.
  • International Labour Organization (ILO) â SME and enterprise development publications â free guides on running small businesses.
  • African Development Bank â Knowledge and SME finance publications â Africa-specific enterprise and financing context.

End of Practical Reference module. Return to this page before every major quote, every new hire, and every equipment purchase.

quiz.q: Why is it important to treat welding as a business, not just a job?
options: A) Because you can charge more per hour
B) Because it allows you to build wealth and employ others
C) Because you don't need to wear safety gear
D) Because you can avoid paying taxes
quiz.explanation: Treating welding as a business enables growth, profitability, and job creation, unlike just selling time.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key reason many welders stay poor?
options: A) They don't know how to weld
B) They only sell their time by the hour and never build a business
C) They refuse to work in cities
D) They only use expensive tools
quiz.explanation: Many welders fail to scale because they focus on hourly work rather than building a sustainable business.

quiz.q: What is a common demand for welding services in African towns?
options: B) Building gates, window frames, and burglar bars
quiz.explanation: Metalwork like gates, window frames, and burglar bars is in constant demand across Africa.

quiz.q: What should you do before buying materials for a job?
options: A) Take a 50% deposit from the customer
B) Buy the most expensive steel
D) Borrow money from a friend
quiz.explanation: A deposit ensures you have funds for materials and reduces the risk of non-payment.

quiz.q: Which of these is a recommended welding machine for a small workshop in Africa?
options: C) A gas welding set only
quiz.explanation: A 200-amp inverter welder is portable, runs on 220V, and is suitable for most small jobs.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an auto-darkening welding helmet?
options: A) To protect your eyes from arc flash
B) To keep your head warm
C) To improve your welding speed
D) To listen to music while welding
quiz.explanation: Auto-darkening helmets automatically darken to protect eyes from harmful arc rays.

quiz.q: Why should you buy steel in bulk?
options: A) To get a discount and ensure you have stock
D) Because it's the only way to buy
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying reduces unit cost and ensures you can start jobs without delay.

quiz.q: What is a good way to transport materials if you can't afford a truck?
options: A) Carry them on your head
C) Ask customers to bring their own
D) Use a wheelbarrow for all jobs
quiz.explanation: A handcart is a low-cost, practical solution for moving steel and finished products.

quiz.q: What is the first step in setting up a welding business?
quiz.explanation: Registering your business allows you to open a bank account, get a tax number, and bid for contracts.

quiz.q: How should you calculate your price for a job?
options: A) Charge whatever the customer offers
B) Add up materials, labour, overhead, and profit margin
C) Use the same price for every job
D) Double the cost of materials
quiz.explanation: A proper price covers all costs and includes a fair profit margin.

quiz.q: What percentage deposit should you ask for before starting a job?
quiz.explanation: A 50% deposit covers material costs and ensures customer commitment.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep business and personal money separate?
options: A) To avoid confusion and track profitability
B) Because the bank requires it
C) To hide money from family
quiz.explanation: Separating funds helps you manage cash flow and know if your business is profitable.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when pricing welding jobs?
quiz.explanation: Undercharging leads to loss of money and inability to cover costs.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer refuses to pay a deposit?
options: B) Politely insist or decline the job
C) Buy materials with your own money
D) Ask for payment after delivery
quiz.explanation: Without a deposit, you risk not being paid and losing money on materials.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important?
options: A) To know your profit and make better decisions
B) To show off to customers
quiz.explanation: Records help you track income, expenses, and profitability.

quiz.q: What should you do if you don't know how to do a job?
options: A) Pretend you can and try anyway
B) Be honest and refer the customer or learn
D) Do a poor job and hope they don't notice
quiz.explanation: Honesty preserves your reputation and may lead to future work.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a quality weld?
options: A) It is smooth, with no undercut, porosity, or cracks
B) It has a lot of spatter
C) It is painted over immediately
quiz.explanation: A good weld is strong, clean, and free of defects.

quiz.q: What PPE is essential for welding?
options: A) Welding helmet, gloves, apron, safety boots
D) No PPE needed if you're careful
quiz.explanation: Proper PPE protects against burns, eye damage, and electric shock.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important when welding?
quiz.explanation: Welding fumes contain harmful gases and metals; ventilation keeps you safe.

quiz.q: What should you keep nearby in case of fire?
options: A) A fire extinguisher or bucket of sand
quiz.explanation: Fire extinguishers or sand can quickly put out small fires caused by sparks.

quiz.q: What amperage range is suitable for a 2.5mm electrode on 3mm steel?
quiz.explanation: 70-90 amps is typical for 2.5mm electrodes on thin steel.

quiz.q: Why should you clean metal before welding?
options: A) To remove rust, paint, and oil for a better weld
quiz.explanation: Clean metal ensures good penetration and avoids defects like porosity.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical exercise?
options: A) Write a one-page business plan
quiz.explanation: A business plan helps you clarify your services, prices, and target market.

quiz.q: How many jobs should you aim to complete in the first month of the exercise?
quiz.explanation: Completing at least three jobs builds experience and confidence.

quiz.q: What should you do after completing a job?
options: A) Ask for a testimonial and post photos
B) Immediately spend all the money
D) Raise your prices without reason
quiz.explanation: Testimonials and photos are powerful marketing tools for future customers.

quiz.q: Why is it important to reinvest profits?
options: A) To grow the business and buy better tools
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting allows you to scale, improve quality, and take on bigger jobs.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when starting a welding business?
quiz.explanation: Business is slow at first; persistence is key to success.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel dizzy while welding?
options: A) Stop and get fresh air immediately
C) Drink water and keep going
quiz.explanation: Dizziness may indicate fume exposure; stop and ventilate.

quiz.q: What is a good way to market your welding business?
options: A) Use social media and word of mouth
B) Wait for customers to come
quiz.explanation: Social media and referrals are low-cost, effective marketing methods.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a defect in your weld?
options: A) Grind it out and re-weld
D) Add more weld on top
quiz.explanation: Defects must be removed and re-welded to ensure strength and safety.
